correctness.rationale: Re-derived the projected ellipse (semiaxes 1,c) and on-minor-axis projected apex hs, and integrated their maximum support function with no factor-of-two ambiguity. In the active interval (α,π−α), cot α=z=√(h²−(1+h²)c²) and s cos α=z/√(1+h²). Moving-boundary terms cancel, giving ∂hP=2z/√(1+h²) and, after division by 2c, the stated J+J₀−B for the c derivative. The h derivative is strictly below the side-on derivative for every c>0, including at activation, so the continuous positive-at-zero difference crosses strictly once and tends to −∞ for fixed c>0 by P≤4E+2hs. In the short-cone argument the derivative of B² as a function of x=c² has sign h²−1−(1+h²)x, so B≤1/√2<π/4≤J for 0<h≤1. NIST DLMF 19.12.2 with complementary modulus k′=c gives the stated expansion; the analytic incomplete-arc correction is uniformly O(c²) on compact positive height intervals. Therefore h_c tends to ∞ at c=0 (use positivity at each fixed large height and the strict crossing), and a continuous crossing family attains its minimum; 1 cannot be the minimizer in c since a nearby inactive ellipse beats the axial tie at h₁. Attainment in the interior then gives the strict height bounds, and the uniform side-on penalty rules out oblique winners near c=0 at the switch. Axial views are excluded at all positive heights by the inactive ellipse comparison. A separate 35-digit support-quadrature calculation obtained the stationary tie c≈0.795726767064798, h≈1.601499304498265; it is not a global or interval certificate. Packaged checker inspected but not executed; the result does not assert uniqueness of the oblique latitude or a certified decimal.

evidence: Vickers–Brown abstract describes distributions of random projected area and joint perimeter/area for convex solid particles, including conical shapes; the frozen bibliography reports the relevant circular-cone analysis/Appendix A is for area, but this review could not independently see that full text.
Finch gives surface area and mean width and their optimization under a change of body, not under changing the viewing direction of a fixed right cone.
DLMF gives the classical elliptic logarithmic term before any projection geometry is imposed.
broader_coverage.reasoning: A full directional perimeter law (or full support of its distribution as the aspect varies) would be materially relevant. The accessible Vickers–Brown material does not show such a circular-cone minimizer theorem; no inference about unread pages is made. Finch and DLMF do not give the single-height crossing or the global/local distinction.

evidence: The bicone has a side-on rhombus and continuous square-root departure; the present cone has a side-on triangle and persistent strict local stability. The maximum brightness theorem extremizes area with a different threshold.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The untruncated elliptic perimeter formula and the projected-hull description do not imply strict relative height monotonicity together with compactness away from zero cosine. These additional steps prove the asserted phase switch. Area, spatial mean width and two-apex perimeter are not equivalent objectives.

evidence: The support integral can equivalently be phrased as planar mean width times π, or as the perimeter of the convex hull of an ellipse and an axial point.
Finch §2 computes the three-dimensional mean width of a cone. Resultary 0f13e384bdf1 concerns the analogous two-apex solid and its continuous onset.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: A body's three-dimensional mean width is not the minimum of its directional planar mean widths. Replacing the apex by two antipodal apices changes the support integral, and the continuous bifurcation for that body is not the discontinuous switch here.

value.rationale: Minimizing the perimeter of an orthogonal silhouette is natural for a canonical convex body. The global jump with strict local persistence on the losing side is stronger than a one-view ellipse formula or a numerical aspect-ratio estimate; the normalized logarithmic barrier explains the qualitative difference from the bicone. The theorem remains useful without a count of oblique minima.
